lead: A signal's shape can be moved along the time axis, squeezed or stretched, and flipped left-to-right — all by changing the independent variable inside the bracket. These three edits are shifting, scaling and reversal. Every delay line, playback-speed change and time-reversed echo is one of them. They also explain why the delay inside x(2t − 1) is 0.5 s, not 1 s. Reading the order correctly earns easy marks and gives correct code in a digital filter.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for the notation x(t) and x[n], and Chapter 1.3 for the pulse and step shapes used here.

sections.h3: Shift: slide the signal along the time axis

blocks.text: Write y(t) = x(t − t₀). Here t₀ is the shift, in seconds. A feature that sits at time t₁ in x(t) sits at t₁ + t₀ in y(t).

For t₀ > 0 every feature moves right, so the signal is delayed. For t₀ < 0 it moves left, so the signal is advanced. A train announcement recorded at 9:00 and played 3 s later is x(t − 3). Only the position changes, never the shape.

Discrete time uses the same rule with an integer shift: y[n] = x[n − n₀], with n₀ a whole number. Samples keep their values and spacing; only their positions change. n₀ must be an integer because x[n] exists only at integer n, so x[n − 0.5] is not defined.
Shifting models every delay: an audio echo, a satellite hop, the queue buffer inside a router, a UPI confirmation that lands two seconds late.

sections.h3: Scale: squeeze or stretch the time axis

blocks.text: Write y(t) = x(at), with a a nonzero real number. The value that x had at t₁ now appears at t = t₁/a.
y(t) = x(at)  →  a feature at t₁ moves to t₁ / a
blocks.where: a is the scale factor; a > 1 compresses time (faster, shorter signal), 0 < a < 1 stretches time (slower, longer signal), and a < 0 combines scaling with reversal.

blocks.text: A four-minute song played at double speed is x(2t); it finishes in two minutes. A pulse of width 2 s becomes a pulse of width 2/a s.

Discrete time needs an integer index, so scaling splits in two. y[n] = x[Mn] with M a positive integer keeps every M-th sample — downsampling, or decimation — and the record becomes M times shorter. Upsampling inserts M − 1 zeros between samples and stretches the record M times. x[Mn] discards samples and can fold high frequencies downwards (Unit 5).
Write y(t) = x(−t). Every feature at t₁ moves to −t₁. A pulse on 0 to 2 s becomes the same pulse on −2 to 0 s, with the same height 2.
x(−t) flips the time axis, not the amplitude. The vertical flip is −x(t), which turns a positive pulse into a negative one. Reversal answers 'when', inversion answers 'how much'.
Reversal appears in playing a recording backwards, in the even part (x(t) + x(−t))/2 from Chapter 1.2, and in correlation, where one signal is reversed before sliding past the other (Unit 2).

sections.h3: Combined operations: choose one order and keep it

blocks.text: A general inside form is x(at − b). Both recipes below are correct; mixing them is the usual mistake.

items: Scale first, then shift. x(at − b) = x(a(t − b/a)). Apply x(at), then delay the result by b/a; if b/a > 0 the move is to the right.
Shift first, then scale. Start from x(t − b), which is x delayed by b seconds, then replace t by at to get x(at − b). The shift stays b, then the whole picture is compressed by a.
Check with the edges. If x is nonzero for A ≤ argument ≤ B, solve A ≤ at − b ≤ B for t.

blocks.text: Both recipes agree when each is followed fully. For x(2t − 1): scale first gives x(2t), then a right shift of 0.5 s; shift first gives a 1 s delay, then compression by 2. The delay in seconds is b/a = 0.5 s, not 1 s.

figure.caption: x(t) is a pulse of height 2 from 0 to 2 s. Compressing by 2 and delaying by 0.5 s gives x(2t − 1) on 0.5 to 1.5 s; reversing and delaying by 1 s gives x(−t + 1) on −1 to 1 s.

spec.aria: A rectangular pulse x(t) from t=0 to 2 of height 2 is compressed and shifted to x(2t-1) on 0.5 to 1.5, and reversed and shifted to x(-t+1) on -1 to 1.

examples.question: A continuous-time signal is x(t) = 2 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 s and x(t) = 0 elsewhere. (a) Find the nonzero time interval and the amplitude of y(t) = x(2t − 1). (b) Find the nonzero time interval and the amplitude of z(t) = x(−t + 1). (c) Sketch both against x(t).
steps: y is nonzero only when the argument lies inside the pulse: 0 ≤ 2t − 1 ≤ 2.
Add 1 to all three parts: 1 ≤ 2t ≤ 3. Divide by 2: 0.5 ≤ t ≤ 1.5 s.
The height is copied, so y(t) = 2 on this interval and 0 outside.
Check: x(2t − 1) = x(2(t − 0.5)) — compress 0–2 s to 0–1 s, then shift right 0.5 s. Agrees.
For z the argument is −t + 1: 0 ≤ −t + 1 ≤ 2 gives −1 ≤ −t ≤ 1, and flipping both inequalities gives −1 ≤ t ≤ 1 s.
z(t) = 2 on −1 ≤ t ≤ 1 s and 0 outside.
Check: x(−t + 1) = x(−(t − 1)) — reverse to −2 to 0 s, then shift right 1 s. Agrees.
Sketch: x(t) is a height-2 rectangle of width 2 s from 0 to 2; y(t) has width 1 s from 0.5 to 1.5 s; z(t) has width 2 s from −1 to 1 s.
examples.answer: y(t) = 2 on 0.5 ≤ t ≤ 1.5 s, and z(t) = 2 on −1 ≤ t ≤ 1 s; both are zero outside, with amplitude 2.

traps: x(2t − 1) does not mean a delay of 1 s. Shifting x right by 1 s gives x(t − 1); replacing t by 2t then gives x(2t − 1), which is the same waveform, but the compression shrinks the 1 s delay to 0.5 s. Compressing first by 2 and then shifting right by 0.5 s gives the same x(2t − 1). Quoting the delay as 1 s is the mistake.
In x(at − b) the delay is b/a seconds, not b.
x(−t) is not −x(t). The first mirrors the signal in time, the second flips it upside down. A pulse on 0 to 2 s becomes a pulse on −2 to 0 s, not a dip on 0 to 2 s.
For discrete time, the shift n₀ must be an integer and the scale M must be a positive integer. x[2n] keeps samples 0, 2, 4, … and is not interpolation; zero insertion is the separate upsampling step.
Sign slip on shifts: x(t + 3) moves the signal 3 s to the left, because the feature at t₁ now occurs at t₁ − 3.

quiz.q: What does the operation x(t − 4) do to a signal?
quiz.a: Delays it by 4 s: every feature moves 4 s to the right. Shape and amplitude do not change.

quiz.q: State the effect of x(3t) and of x(t/3) on the time axis.
quiz.a: x(3t) compresses time by a factor of 3. x(t/3) stretches time by a factor of 3.

quiz.q: Why is it useful to rewrite x(2t − 1) as x(2(t − 0.5))?
quiz.a: It shows the correct pair of operations in order: compress by 2, then delay by 0.5 s. It also states the delay in seconds directly, which is b/a = 0.5 s.

quiz.q: x(t) = 1 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 s and 0 elsewhere. Find the nonzero interval and amplitude of y(t) = x(−2t + 1).
quiz.a: Solve 0 ≤ −2t + 1 ≤ 1: subtract 1 gives −1 ≤ −2t ≤ 0, divide by −2 and flip gives 0 ≤ t ≤ 0.5 s. Amplitude stays 1. Check: x(−2t + 1) = x(−2(t − 0.5)) — reverse, compress by 2, shift right by 0.5 s.

quiz.q: x[n] = 1 for 0 ≤ n ≤ 5 and 0 elsewhere. Give the nonzero samples of y[n] = x[2n].
quiz.a: 0 ≤ 2n ≤ 5 gives 0 ≤ n ≤ 2.5, so only n = 0, 1, 2 survive, with 2n = 0, 2, 4. y[0] = y[1] = y[2] = 1 and y[n] = 0 for all other n. Three of the six ones are discarded.

quiz.q: A student says x(2t − 4) is a delay of 4 s followed by compression by 2, so the delay stays 4 s. Identify the mistake and give the correct delay in seconds.
quiz.a: The operations are right but the delay is not. Replacing t by 2t in x(t − 4) leaves the inside as x(2t − 4), and the actual delay in the final signal is 4/2 = 2 s, since x(2t − 4) = x(2(t − 2)).

quiz.q: Distinguish x(−t) from −x(t) for a pulse of height 2 on 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 s.
quiz.a: x(−t) is the same positive pulse of height 2 on −2 ≤ t ≤ 0 s (time mirror). −x(t) is a pulse of height −2 on 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 s (amplitude inversion).

quiz.q: x(t) is even and is nonzero on −1 ≤ t ≤ 1 s. Is y(t) = x(2t − 1) even? Justify.
quiz.a: No. y(−t) = x(−2t − 1) = x(2t + 1) because x is even, and x(2t + 1) is not equal to x(2t − 1) in general. Also y is nonzero where −1 ≤ 2t − 1 ≤ 1, i.e. 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 s, which is symmetric about 0.5 s, not about 0. Evenness survives reversal but not a shift.

beyond: Not for the exam. In software radio and audio DSP these edits become multirate processing: decimation by M is x[Mn] after an anti-alias filter, and interpolation inserts zeros then low-pass filters them (the filters sit in Unit 5). Image processing applies the same rules to pixel indices — shifting crops, scaling resizes, reversal mirrors. Radar correlators use reversal, because a matched filter compares the echo with a time-reversed copy of the transmitted pulse. Search 'multirate signal processing' and 'fractional delay filter' to continue.
